newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian miners keep watch on silver price.
newsitem.headline: Australian miners keep watch on silver price.

text.p: Australian silver producers are keeping an eye on the lower silver price in the wake of tumbling gold prices, but say demand fundamentals remain good.
Spot silver fell through long-term support at US$4.60 an ounce in line with the plunge in gold last week and fixed at US$4.25 in London on Tuesday morning, its lowest fix in four years.

"The export market is pretty healthy so we are not overly concerned at the moment," said Pasminco Ltd senior business analyst David Whelan on Wednesday, adding that demand remained strong out of India.
Pasminco and MIM Holdings Ltd produce the bulk of Australia's silver, but as a by-product of lead and zinc mining, while some silver production is linked to gold mining.

MIM produced about 12.5 million ounces of silver in 1995/96 from its Mt Isa mine in Queensland, at one time the largest single silver producing mine in the world, while Pasminco produced about 8.2 million ounces.
In all, about 32.76 million ounces of silver was produced in Australia in 1995/96, according to the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Statistics (ABARE).
This compared with world production of about 441 million ounces in calendar 1995.
Macquarie Equities base metals analyst Will Corkhill said silver provided a credit for the two companies, but their leverage to the silver price was relatively small.

For Pasminco, a 10-percent drop in the price of silver over one year would cause a 0.3-cent drop in earnings per share (EPS), compared with a 5.4-cent EPS hit for a similar decline in the zinc price, Corkhill said.
At an average price of US$4.60 an ounce, silver would have contributed about US$77 million to MIM's total annual revenue of A$2.58 billion in 1995/96.
MIM spokesman Collin Myers said a 10-percent change in the price of silver, sustained over 12 months, would add or detract about A$5 million from MIM's earnings.
This compared with a A$28 million change for a similar rise or fall in the price of copper.
"It's a useful and important metal but its not the main metal," Myers said.
